lessons.title: Vasomotor symptoms: burden, mechanism and identification
lessons.objective: Describe the frequency, duration and impact of VMS, explain their hypothalamic mechanism (KNDy neurons and neurokinin B) and identify perimenopause and menopause clinically according to NICE NG23, knowing which tests not to order.
lessons.closing: Hot flashes are common, last for years and have a known hypothalamic mechanism. From age 45, perimenopause and menopause are recognised clinically: AMH, estradiol and other hormone tests do not change the decision, and saliva or urine tests are not reliable for setting hormone therapy doses either.

lessons.title: Hormone therapy: benefits, risks, route and “bioidenticals”
lessons.objective: Prescribe hormone therapy as the most effective treatment for VMS, choose the regimen by whether there is a uterus, choose the route by thrombotic risk, explain breast cancer risk in numbers, compare the initiation “window” and duration in NICE and NAMS, and answer requests for compounded “bioidenticals” with evidence.
lessons.closing: With a uterus, always a progestogen; with thrombotic risk, the transdermal route; and risks in absolute numbers. NICE and NAMS agree on the essentials and differ on nuances: the coronary “window” and the emphasis on the lowest dose. Approved bioidenticals already exist; compounding adds no safety.

lessons.title: Without hormones: psychological therapies, drugs, supplements and lifestyle
lessons.objective: Offer evidence-backed alternatives for those who cannot or will not take HRT (CBT, clinical hypnosis, SSRIs/SNRIs, gabapentin, fezolinetant), know their doses and precautions, such as the tamoxifen interaction, and explain why NAMS does not recommend black cohosh, soy or most supplements and lifestyle measures, noting where NICE differs.
lessons.closing: Without hormones there are real options: CBT and clinical hypnosis, SSRIs/SNRIs, gabapentin and fezolinetant. Supplements, soy and lifestyle changes have little support for hot flashes, and where NICE is more permissive, its wording dates from 2015.

items.title: Vasomotor symptoms: common, long-lasting and with impact
items.core: Hot flashes and night sweats (vasomotor symptoms, VMS) are the most common symptoms of menopause: they occur in up to 80% of women and last a mean of 7 to 9 years; in one-third, more than 10 years. [[ref:nams-2023-nonhormone-therapy]]
items.body:
The 2022 NAMS position statement notes that VMS may begin in perimenopause, that frequent VMS persist on average 7.4 years or longer, that they affect quality of life and that they may be associated with cardiovascular, bone and brain health. Women with VMS more often report disrupted sleep. [[ref:nams-2022-hormone-therapy]]

NICE identifies perimenopause, without laboratory tests, in healthy people aged 45 or over with recently started VMS and changes in their menstrual cycle. [[ref:nice-2026-ng23]]
items.recall: In what proportion of women do VMS occur, and how long do they last on average?
items.pearl: When a patient asks “how long will this last?”, the honest answer is: on average, years; in one in three, more than a decade.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: NAMS 2023: figures from the introductory text (no level). NAMS 2022: duration and associations of VMS, Level I/II; disrupted sleep with VMS, Level I. NICE NG23 1.3.1 [2015]. NAMS (now The Menopause Society) levels: I = good and consistent scientific evidence; II = limited or inconsistent scientific evidence; III = primarily consensus and expert opinion. NICE assigns no evidence levels to its recommendations; in brackets, the year each was made or updated.

items.title: KNDy neurons and neurokinin B: why hot flashes happen
items.core: Hypothalamic KNDy neurons (kisspeptin, neurokinin B and dynorphin) form the GnRH pulse generator and also act on the adjacent thermoregulatory centre. As estradiol falls across the transition, this plexus becomes hyperactive and hypersecretes neurokinin B, which disrupts temperature control and triggers VMS. [[ref:nams-2023-nonhormone-therapy]]
items.body: This understanding led to neurokinin B antagonists, which target the neural mechanism of VMS directly. Fezolinetant is a selective neurokinin B receptor-3 antagonist approved by the FDA; elinzanetant, a dual receptor-1 and receptor-3 antagonist, was in development in 2023, and a third compound (MLE4901) is no longer being pursued for this indication. [[ref:nams-2023-nonhormone-therapy]]
items.recall: Which neurons and which neuropeptide explain VMS, and which drug acts on that step?
items.application: Regulatory update: the EU authorised elinzanetant (Lynkuet 60 mg) in November 2025 for moderate to severe vasomotor symptoms. CIMA lists it as authorised but not marketed in Spain as of 14 October 2026. [[ref:ema-2025-lynkuet-epar]]
items.pearl: This is why a non-hormonal drug can relieve hot flashes “from the hypothalamus” without supplying estrogen.

evidence.label: mechanistic
evidence.note: NAMS 2023, section on neurokinin B antagonists: explanatory text (no level). US regulatory status in 2023. NAMS (now The Menopause Society) levels: I = good and consistent scientific evidence; II = limited or inconsistent scientific evidence; III = primarily consensus and expert opinion.

items.title: Perimenopause and menopause: identified clinically
items.core: NICE recommends identifying, without laboratory tests, in healthy people aged 45 or over with symptoms: perimenopause if there are recently started VMS and cycle changes; menopause if there has been no period for at least 12 months without hormonal contraception; and, after a hysterectomy, menopause based on the type and combination of symptoms. [[ref:nice-2026-ng23]]
items.body: FSH is only considered to confirm menopause between 40 and 45 with symptoms, including a cycle change, or under 40 if it is suspected (see the premature ovarian insufficiency module). NICE warns that it is difficult to identify in people on hormonal treatments, for example for heavy menstrual bleeding, and that some people from ethnic minority backgrounds or with lifelong conditions may reach it at a younger age. [[ref:nice-2026-ng23]]
items.recall: When does NICE identify perimenopause and menopause without tests, and when does it consider FSH?
items.application: Faced with a 47-year-old with recent hot flashes and lengthening cycles, the diagnosis is clinical: ask, record the symptoms and move on to discussing options.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: NICE NG23 1.3.1 [2015], 1.3.2 [2015], 1.3.3 [2024] and 1.3.6 [2015]. NICE assigns no evidence levels to its recommendations; in brackets, the year each was made or updated.

items.title: Tests that add nothing: AMH, estradiol, saliva and urine
items.core: To identify perimenopause or menopause from age 45, NICE advises against using AMH, inhibin A, inhibin B, estradiol, antral follicle count or ovarian volume. [[ref:nice-2026-ng23]]
items.body:
Nor should FSH be used to identify menopause in people taking combined estrogen and progestogen contraception or high-dose progestogen. [[ref:nice-2026-ng23]]

To set hormone therapy doses, NAMS considers saliva and urine hormone testing unreliable and does not recommend it, and regards serum testing as rarely needed. [[ref:nams-2022-hormone-therapy]]
items.recall: Which tests does NICE advise against for identifying menopause from age 45?
items.pearl: A “menopause hormone panel” at 50 does not change the decision; the clinical picture does.

evidence.label: not-recommended
evidence.note: NICE NG23 1.3.4 and 1.3.5 [2015]. NAMS 2022: saliva, urine and serum testing, Level II/III. NICE assigns no evidence levels to its recommendations; in brackets, the year each was made or updated. NAMS (now The Menopause Society) levels: I = good and consistent scientific evidence; II = limited or inconsistent scientific evidence; III = primarily consensus and expert opinion.

items.stem: A 48-year-old woman (fictional case), healthy and not using hormonal contraception, has had hot flashes for 3 months and cycles every 45–60 days. According to NICE NG23, what is most appropriate?

options.text: Identify perimenopause clinically, without tests, and discuss options.
options.why: Correct: from age 45, recently started VMS and cycle changes are enough for NICE.

options.text: Order FSH and estradiol on cycle day 3 to confirm it.
options.why: NICE advises against estradiol at this age and reserves FSH for ages 40–45 or under 40.

options.text: Order AMH to estimate how long until menopause.
options.why: AMH is among the tests NICE advises against from age 45.

options.text: Wait for 12 months of amenorrhoea before discussing treatment.
options.why: Twelve months without a period identify menopause; perimenopause is already identified with these symptoms and options can be discussed.

items.explanation: NICE aims to avoid tests that do not change the decision: in healthy people aged 45 or over, perimenopause and menopause are identified by symptoms and menstrual pattern.

items.stem: According to the 2023 NAMS position statement, which mechanism explains VMS and is the target of fezolinetant?

options.text: Hyperactivity of KNDy neurons, with excess neurokinin B acting on the thermoregulatory centre.
options.why: Correct: fezolinetant blocks the neurokinin B receptor-3.

options.text: The rise in FSH, acting directly on the thermoregulatory centre.
options.why: FSH rises through the pulse generator, but the statement attributes VMS to neurokinin B, not FSH.

options.text: A serotonin deficit in the cerebral cortex.
options.why: SSRIs/SNRIs relieve VMS, but the mechanism described, and fezolinetant’s target, is hypothalamic neurokinin B.

options.text: Excess orexin, which fezolinetant blocks.
options.why: Orexin is mentioned as possibly involved, but fezolinetant does not act on it and suvorexant is not recommended.

items.explanation: As estradiol falls, the KNDy plexus hypersecretes neurokinin B onto the thermoregulatory centre; neurokinin B antagonists act at exactly that step.

items.title: Hormone therapy: the most effective treatment for VMS
items.core: NICE recommends offering hormone replacement therapy (HRT) to people with menopausal VMS. [[ref:nice-2026-ng23]] NAMS considers it the most effective treatment for VMS and the genitourinary syndrome of menopause, and it also prevents bone loss and fracture; the various formulations, doses and routes of prescription preparations have comparably high efficacy for VMS. [[ref:nams-2022-hormone-therapy]]
items.body:
Before starting, NICE asks for a discussion of the benefits and risks of combined versus estrogen-only HRT, transdermal versus oral routes, types of estrogen and progestogen, sequential versus continuous regimens, and dose and duration, tailored to each person’s age and risk factors. [[ref:nice-2026-ng23]]

NAMS lists as contraindications to oral and transdermal therapy unexplained vaginal bleeding, liver disease, prior estrogen-sensitive cancer (including breast cancer), prior coronary heart disease, stroke, myocardial infarction or venous thromboembolism, and a personal history or inherited high risk of thromboembolic disease. [[ref:nams-2022-hormone-therapy]]
items.recall: What does NICE recommend for menopausal VMS, and which contraindications to hormone therapy does NAMS list?
items.pearl: Without a contraindication, the question is not “HRT, yes or no?” but “which HRT, by which route and at what dose for this woman?”.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: NICE NG23 1.5.1 [2015] and 1.4.2 [2024]. NAMS 2022: comparable efficacy of formulations, doses and routes, Level I; “most effective treatment”, conclusion of the statement; contraindications, statement text (no level). NICE assigns no evidence levels to its recommendations; in brackets, the year each was made or updated. NAMS (now The Menopause Society) levels: I = good and consistent scientific evidence; II = limited or inconsistent scientific evidence; III = primarily consensus and expert opinion.

items.title: Age at initiation: the NAMS “window” and NICE’s caution
items.core: NAMS places the most favourable balance in women starting hormone therapy before 60 or within 10 years of menopause onset, without contraindications; when started later, the balance appears less favourable because of greater absolute risks of coronary heart disease, stroke, venous thromboembolism and dementia. [[ref:nams-2022-hormone-therapy]]
items.body:
For NAMS, the effect on coronary heart disease may vary with age or time since menopause at initiation; observational data and meta-analyses show less coronary heart disease when it is started before 60 or within 10 years of menopause, although the effect is null after excluding open-label trials. Hormone therapy is not approved for cardioprotection. [[ref:nams-2022-hormone-therapy]]

NICE sets no such window: its committee found little data and no clear trend in coronary risk with age at initiation or time since menopause, and left it as a research question. It does explain that combined HRT does not increase coronary heart disease risk, that life expectancy is unlikely to change, that dementia risk might increase if started at 65 or over, and that the increase in stroke with oral estrogen is greater with older age at first use. [[ref:nice-2026-ng23]]
items.recall: What initiation “window” does NAMS propose, and what did NICE conclude about timing and coronary risk?
items.pearl: They agree that some risks grow the later treatment starts; they differ on whether a coronary “window” is proven: NAMS supports it and NICE leaves it as an open question.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: NAMS 2022: most favourable safety before 60 or within 10 years, Level I; coronary effect depending on timing of initiation, Level I; less coronary heart disease in observational data, Level II; greater absolute risks with later initiation, Level I; not approved for cardioprotection, Level I. NICE NG23 1.6.1 and table 1 [2024]; rationale on timing of initiation (pp. 82–83) and research recommendation 6. NAMS (now The Menopause Society) levels: I = good and consistent scientific evidence; II = limited or inconsistent scientific evidence; III = primarily consensus and expert opinion. NICE assigns no evidence levels to its recommendations; in brackets, the year each was made or updated.

items.title: With a uterus, always a progestogen
items.core: NICE recommends offering combined HRT to people with a uterus and estrogen-only HRT to people who have had a total hysterectomy. [[ref:nice-2026-ng23]] Unopposed systemic estrogen in a postmenopausal woman with a uterus increases the risk of endometrial cancer, so adequate progestogen is recommended. [[ref:nams-2022-hormone-therapy]]
items.body:
NICE describes endometrial cancer risk as decreasing with continuous combined HRT and possibly increasing slightly with sequential HRT, especially with longer use, fewer days of progestogen per cycle and higher estrogen dosage. [[ref:nice-2026-ng23]]

NAMS cites the combination of conjugated estrogens with bazedoxifene as the only exception. As an example of an adequate dose it gives oral micronized progesterone 200 mg/day for 12–14 days a month. A levonorgestrel IUD for endometrial protection is an off-label use with limited trial data, which avoids systemic progestogen effects and provides contraception for those starting before their final menstrual period. Low-dose vaginal estrogen does not appear to increase endometrial cancer risk, although trials with endometrial biopsy end points last only 1 year. [[ref:nams-2022-hormone-therapy]]

NICE explains that vaginal bleeding is a common side effect during the first 6 months of systemic HRT or within 3 months of a dose or preparation change, and asks people to seek help promptly for unscheduled bleeding beyond these timeframes. [[ref:nice-2026-ng23]]
items.recall: Which HRT applies with and without a uterus, and what micronized progesterone dose does NAMS give as an example?
items.application: In Spain, the product information for Mirena and Levosert (52 mg levonorgestrel IUDs) covers contraception and menorrhagia or heavy menstrual bleeding, but not endometrial protection during HRT: in Spain too, this is an off-label use. [[ref:aemps-2026-mirena-ft]]
items.pearl: Every time you prescribe systemic estrogen, the first question is: does she have a uterus?

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: NICE NG23 1.8.1 [2024]; table 1, endometrial cancer [2024]; 1.8.4 [2015, amended 2026]. NAMS 2022: adequate progestogen, Level I; low-dose vaginal estrogen, Level II; progesterone dose and levonorgestrel IUD, statement text (no level). NICE assigns no evidence levels to its recommendations; in brackets, the year each was made or updated. NAMS (now The Menopause Society) levels: I = good and consistent scientific evidence; II = limited or inconsistent scientific evidence; III = primarily consensus and expert opinion.

items.title: Transdermal or oral: thrombosis and stroke
items.core: For NICE, transdermal HRT does not increase venous thromboembolism (VTE) risk, oral HRT does, and the risk is greater with oral than with transdermal HRT. Stroke risk is unlikely to increase with combined HRT containing transdermal estrogen, whereas with oral estrogen it increases, more so with higher dosage, longer use and older age at first use. [[ref:nice-2026-ng23]]
items.body:
NICE recommends considering transdermal rather than oral HRT when VTE risk is increased, including a BMI over 30 kg/m², and considering referral to a haematologist before HRT when risk is high, such as with a strong family history or hereditary thrombophilia. [[ref:nice-2026-ng23]]

NAMS is more cautious about the evidence: observational studies have not shown increased VTE with transdermal estrogen and suggest less risk than with oral estrogen, but comparative trials are lacking; non-oral routes bypass the hepatic first pass, but it is unknown whether they lower VTE, breast cancer or cardiovascular events. Micronized progesterone may be less thrombogenic than other progestins. [[ref:nams-2022-hormone-therapy]]
items.recall: What does NICE say about VTE and stroke by HRT route, and when does it propose transdermal HRT?
items.pearl: Same practical conclusion (transdermal if there is thrombotic risk) with different certainty: NICE states it; NAMS reminds us it rests on observational studies.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: NICE NG23 table 1: VTE [2015], stroke [2024]; 1.5.28 and 1.5.29 [2015]. NAMS 2022: different effects by dose, formulation and route, Level II; the rest, statement text (no level). NICE assigns no evidence levels to its recommendations; in brackets, the year each was made or updated. NAMS (now The Menopause Society) levels: I = good and consistent scientific evidence; II = limited or inconsistent scientific evidence; III = primarily consensus and expert opinion.

items.title: Breast cancer: explaining the risk with numbers
items.core: NICE explains that combined HRT increases breast cancer risk: more with longer use and more in current than past users; it declines after stopping but persists for at least 10 years. It is lower with sequential than continuous combined HRT (though higher than without HRT), and with estrogen-only HRT there is very little or no increase. [[ref:nice-2026-ng23]]
items.body:
NAMS describes this risk as rare: fewer than one additional case per 1,000 women per year of use, or three additional cases per 1,000 women over 5 years with conjugated equine estrogens plus medroxyprogesterone acetate. It suggests putting this in perspective, as it is similar to modifiable risk factors such as two alcoholic drinks a day, obesity or low physical activity. [[ref:nams-2022-hormone-therapy]]

NICE notes that there is insufficient evidence to know whether the increase differs with micronized progesterone or dydrogesterone compared with other progestogens, and asks clinicians to use its discussion aid, with cases per 1,000 people over 5 and 10 years. [[ref:nice-2026-ng23]]
items.recall: How does breast cancer risk change with duration, regimen and type of HRT, and what size does NAMS give?
items.pearl: “With combined HRT, breast cancer risk rises a little and grows with years of use; to give you an idea, it is similar to having two drinks a day. We will review it together every year.”

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: NICE NG23 1.6.2 and 1.6.3 [2024]; tables 1 and 2, breast cancer [2024]. NAMS 2022: size of the risk, Level I; comparison with modifiable factors, Level III. The patient phrase is an editorial suggestion, not text from the sources. NICE assigns no evidence levels to its recommendations; in brackets, the year each was made or updated. NAMS (now The Menopause Society) levels: I = good and consistent scientific evidence; II = limited or inconsistent scientific evidence; III = primarily consensus and expert opinion.

items.title: Dose, duration and stopping: NICE versus NAMS
items.core: NICE asks for the lowest effective dosage, a discussion of possible duration at the outset, and review of each treatment at 3 months and then annually. [[ref:nice-2026-ng23]] NAMS speaks of the “appropriate, often lowest, effective dose” for the treatment goals, and states that hormone therapy does not need to be routinely discontinued in women older than 60 or 65. [[ref:nams-2022-hormone-therapy]]
items.body:
For NAMS, long-term use, including after 60, may be considered in healthy women at low risk of cardiovascular disease and breast cancer with persistent VMS or high fracture risk for whom other therapies are not appropriate, with periodic reevaluation and periodic trials of lowering or stopping. Mitigating risk with the lowest effective dose and possibly a non-oral route becomes more important with age and longer duration. [[ref:nams-2022-hormone-therapy]]

When stopping, NICE recommends offering a choice between gradual reduction and stopping immediately: gradual reduction may limit symptom recurrence in the short term, but makes no difference in the longer term. Symptoms may return when HRT is stopped, and it can be restarted if needed. [[ref:nice-2026-ng23]]
items.recall: What do NICE and NAMS say about HRT dose, review and stopping after 60–65?
items.pearl: In what was reviewed, neither sets a maximum duration; the nuance is in the wording: NICE asks for the lowest effective dosage; NAMS for the appropriate (often lowest) dose for the goal, giving the lowest dose more weight as age and duration increase.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: NICE NG23 1.8.3 [2024], 1.4.3 [2024], 1.9.2 [2015], 1.8.6 and 1.8.7 [2015]. NAMS 2022: appropriate dose, Level III; no routine discontinuation, long-term use and reevaluation, Level III. NICE assigns no evidence levels to its recommendations; in brackets, the year each was made or updated. NAMS (now The Menopause Society) levels: I = good and consistent scientific evidence; II = limited or inconsistent scientific evidence; III = primarily consensus and expert opinion.

items.title: Myth: compounded “bioidentical” hormones are more natural and safer
items.core: “Bioidentical” can mislead: there are approved, regulated bioidentical hormones (estradiol, estrone, micronized progesterone) and compounded preparations that may combine several hormones (estradiol, estrone, estriol, DHEA, testosterone, progesterone) in untested combinations, formulations or routes, such as subdermal implants, pellets or troches. [[ref:nams-2022-hormone-therapy]]
items.body:
NAMS notes that compounded preparations raise safety concerns: minimal regulation and monitoring, overdosing and underdosing, impurities and lack of sterility, lack of efficacy and safety data, and no label outlining risks. Patient preference alone should not justify their use; they should be considered only when an approved product cannot be used, for example because of allergy to one of its ingredients or because the dose or formulation needed is not available in approved products. [[ref:nams-2022-hormone-therapy]]

NICE asks clinicians to explain that the efficacy and safety of unregulated hormone preparations are unknown. [[ref:nice-2026-ng23]]
items.recall: Which safety concerns does NAMS attribute to compounded “bioidenticals”, and when could they be considered?
items.application: Authorised options: in Spain, oral micronized progesterone (Progeffik 100 and 200 mg) is licensed as an adjunct to estrogen in women with a uterus, and Bijuva combines estradiol 1 mg and progesterone 100 mg. In Argentina, ANMAT’s national formulary includes Utrogestan (micronized progesterone 100 and 200 mg). [[ref:aemps-2026-progeffik-bijuva]] [[ref:anmat-2026-vnm]]
items.pearl: If what she wants is a hormone “identical to her own”, approved estradiol and micronized progesterone already are, with quality control.

evidence.label: not-recommended
evidence.note: NAMS 2022: safety concerns with compounded preparations, Level I; preference alone does not justify them, Level III; situations in which they could be considered, Level III. NICE NG23 1.4.5 [2015]. NAMS (now The Menopause Society) levels: I = good and consistent scientific evidence; II = limited or inconsistent scientific evidence; III = primarily consensus and expert opinion. NICE assigns no evidence levels to its recommendations; in brackets, the year each was made or updated.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman (fictional case) with a uterus and bothersome VMS wants systemic HRT. According to NICE and NAMS, which regimen applies?

options.text: Estrogen with adequate progestogen (combined HRT).
options.why: Correct: NICE offers combined HRT with a uterus, and NAMS recommends adequate progestogen (Level I).

options.text: Transdermal estrogen alone, because the transdermal route protects the endometrium.
options.why: The route does not protect: NICE states that, with a uterus, estrogen alone increases endometrial cancer by both oral and transdermal routes.

options.text: Estrogen alone with an annual endometrial ultrasound.
options.why: Neither source proposes ultrasound surveillance as an alternative to progestogen.

options.text: Micronized progesterone alone, without estrogen.
options.why: NAMS reports that it reduces VMS, but without long-term data and off-label (Level II); it is not the standard regimen.

items.explanation: The progestogen is not for the hot flashes but to protect the endometrium from systemic estrogen; that is why estrogen-only HRT is reserved for those without a uterus.

items.stem: A 50-year-old woman (fictional case), with a BMI of 33 kg/m² and no personal or family history of thrombosis, is about to start HRT for VMS. According to NICE, what is most appropriate?

options.text: Consider the transdermal rather than the oral route.
options.why: Correct: NICE proposes it when VTE risk is increased, including a BMI over 30 kg/m².

options.text: Low-dose oral HRT, which carries the same VTE risk as transdermal.
options.why: NICE states more VTE with oral than transdermal HRT; NAMS notes lower oral doses may carry less risk, without comparative trials.

options.text: Do not prescribe HRT: a BMI over 30 kg/m² contraindicates it.
options.why: NICE does not treat it as a contraindication, but as a reason to choose the route.

options.text: Refer to haematology before any HRT.
options.why: NICE reserves referral for high risk, such as a strong family history or hereditary thrombophilia.

items.explanation: Obesity raises baseline VTE risk; according to NICE the transdermal route does not increase it, whereas the oral route does. NAMS agrees on the direction, while noting the evidence is observational.

items.stem: A 66-year-old woman (fictional case), who reached menopause at 51 and has never had treatment, asks to start systemic HRT for persistent hot flashes. According to NAMS, which statement is correct?

options.text: The benefit-risk balance appears less favourable than in a younger woman and requires careful weighing of her individual benefits and risks.
options.why: Correct: when started after 60 or more than 10 years from menopause, absolute risks of coronary heart disease, stroke, VTE and dementia are greater.

options.text: It is contraindicated from age 65.
options.why: NAMS does not contraindicate it by age: it asks for careful individual assessment.

options.text: Starting it now will protect her from myocardial infarction.
options.why: With late initiation absolute coronary risk is greater, and hormone therapy is not approved for cardioprotection (Level I).

options.text: Age at initiation does not affect any risk.
options.why: It does according to NAMS, and NICE also notes more dementia if started at 65 or over and more stroke with oral estrogen at older starting age.

items.explanation: The NAMS “window” (under 60 or within 10 years of menopause) is not a prohibition outside it, but a shift in the balance that requires individualisation.

items.stem: A 53-year-old patient (fictional case) asks for “bioidentical hormones” as pellets, dosed by a saliva test, because she believes they are more natural. According to NAMS, what is most appropriate?

options.text: Explain that approved estradiol and micronized progesterone are already bioidentical and regulated, and that saliva testing cannot guide dosing.
options.why: Correct: NAMS considers compounded preparations a safety concern (Level I) and saliva testing unreliable (Level II/III).

options.text: Agree: patient preference justifies the compounded preparation.
options.why: For NAMS, preference alone does not justify a compounded product when regulated ones are available (Level III).

options.text: Agree, but adjust the dose with a urine test instead of saliva.
options.why: NAMS considers both saliva and urine testing unreliable and does not recommend them.

options.text: Prefer pellets because they give more stable levels.
options.why: NAMS lists pellets among nonstandard or untested routes; it does not credit them with that advantage.

items.explanation: Shared decision-making matters, but offering hormones identical to her own does not require compounding: approved products already are, with quality control and a label. NICE adds that the efficacy and safety of unregulated preparations are unknown.

items.stem: According to the 2022 NAMS position statement, how is the size of the breast cancer risk associated with hormone therapy described?

options.text: Rare: fewer than one additional case per 1,000 women per year of use.
options.why: Correct: NAMS gives this figure (Level I) and compares it with factors such as two alcoholic drinks a day.

options.text: Common: more than 10 additional cases per 1,000 women per year.
options.why: NAMS classifies it as rare, far below that figure.

options.text: Zero with any combined regimen.
options.why: Both NAMS and NICE describe an increase with combined HRT, which grows with duration.

options.text: The same with estrogen alone as with combined therapy.
options.why: NICE describes very little or no increase with estrogen alone, and in the WHI conjugated estrogens alone were associated with less breast cancer.

items.explanation: Speaking in absolute risks helps decision-making: a real but rare increase, greater with combined therapy and with more years of use.

items.title: CBT and clinical hypnosis: the best-supported non-drug options
items.core: NAMS recommends cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) and clinical hypnosis for VMS, both at Level I. [[ref:nams-2023-nonhormone-therapy]] NICE recommends considering menopause-specific CBT as an option for VMS, alongside HRT, when HRT is contraindicated or when people prefer not to take it. [[ref:nice-2026-ng23]]
items.body:
According to NICE, CBT improved frequency, severity and, above all, how much symptoms bothered people, although the evidence had design limitations and potential bias. [[ref:nice-2026-ng23]]

NAMS notes that CBT studies mostly use waitlist or usual-care controls, which are less rigorous, and that overall they support relief of bothersome VMS in breast cancer survivors and menopausal women. In one trial, clinical hypnosis reduced hot flash frequency by 74% versus 17% with an attention control; it can be delivered by a trained provider or through a smartphone app. By contrast, it does not recommend paced respiration (Level I) or relaxation or mindfulness (Level II). [[ref:nams-2023-nonhormone-therapy]]
items.recall: Which psychological interventions do NAMS and NICE recommend for VMS, and which does NAMS not recommend?
items.pearl: They are real options for those who cannot or will not take HRT, and also add-ons: CBT acts mainly on how bothersome the hot flashes are.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: NAMS 2023: CBT and clinical hypnosis, Level I, recommended; paced respiration, Level I, not recommended; relaxation and mindfulness, Level II, not recommended. NICE NG23 1.5.2 [2024] and its rationale (p. 60). NG23 does not address hypnosis. NAMS (now The Menopause Society) levels: I = good and consistent scientific evidence; II = limited or inconsistent scientific evidence; III = primarily consensus and expert opinion. NICE assigns no evidence levels to its recommendations; in brackets, the year each was made or updated.

items.title: Non-hormonal drugs: SSRIs/SNRIs, gabapentin and fezolinetant
items.core: NAMS recommends SSRIs/SNRIs, gabapentin and fezolinetant (Level I) and oxybutynin (Levels I-II); it does not recommend clonidine, pregabalin or suvorexant. [[ref:nams-2023-nonhormone-therapy]] NICE advises against routinely offering SSRIs, SNRIs or clonidine as first-line treatment for VMS alone, and recommends fezolinetant as an option for moderate to severe VMS when HRT is unsuitable. [[ref:nice-2026-ng23]]
items.body:
Doses from the NAMS table: paroxetine salt 7.5 mg/day (FDA approved for VMS); paroxetine 10–25 mg/day; citalopram and escitalopram 10–20 mg/day; venlafaxine 37.5–150 mg/day; desvenlafaxine 100–150 mg/day; gabapentin 900–2,400 mg/day in divided doses; fezolinetant 45 mg/day. SSRIs/SNRIs give mild to moderate improvements; with sertraline and fluoxetine improvements were not significant and they are not recommended. [[ref:nams-2023-nonhormone-therapy]]

With tamoxifen, paroxetine and fluoxetine may inhibit CYP2D6, which converts it to its active metabolite; NAMS suggests venlafaxine, desvenlafaxine, escitalopram or citalopram as safer choices. Gabapentin causes dizziness and drowsiness at first, so bedtime dosing may suit women whose night-time VMS disrupt sleep; long-term oxybutynin may be associated with cognitive decline in older people. In the phase 3 trials available in 2023, headache was the most common adverse event with neurokinin B antagonists, and liver enzyme elevation was rare and resolved during continued treatment or after stopping it. [[ref:nams-2023-nonhormone-therapy]]
items.recall: Which non-hormonal drugs does NAMS recommend, where does NICE differ, and which SSRIs to avoid with tamoxifen?
items.application: In Spain and the EU, the Veoza product information requires liver tests before starting, monthly for the first 3 months and then as clinically indicated; do not start if ALT or AST is ≥ 2 times the upper limit or total bilirubin is elevated. The FDA label adds a boxed warning for hepatotoxicity and checks at 6 and 9 months. [[ref:aemps-2026-veoza-ft]] [[ref:fda-2026-veozah-label]]
items.pearl: A real disagreement: for NAMS, SSRIs/SNRIs are a Level I option; for NICE (2015 wording) they are not first line for VMS alone. On fezolinetant they agree, NICE when HRT is unsuitable.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: NAMS 2023: SSRIs/SNRIs, gabapentin and fezolinetant, Level I, recommended; oxybutynin, Levels I-II, recommended; clonidine, Levels I-III, pregabalin, Level III, and suvorexant, Level II, not recommended; doses from table 1 (p. 6). NICE NG23 1.5.3 (refers to technology appraisal TA1143, 2026, not reviewed here) and 1.5.4 [2015]. NAMS (now The Menopause Society) levels: I = good and consistent scientific evidence; II = limited or inconsistent scientific evidence; III = primarily consensus and expert opinion. NICE assigns no evidence levels to its recommendations; in brackets, the year each was made or updated.

items.title: Black cohosh, soy and other supplements: what each source says
items.core: NAMS does not recommend supplements or herbal remedies for VMS: black cohosh at Level I, for insufficient evidence; soy, soy extracts and equol at Level II, for mixed evidence. [[ref:nams-2023-nonhormone-therapy]] NICE, with 2015 wording, asks clinicians to explain that there is some evidence that isoflavones or black cohosh may relieve VMS, but that many preparations exist, their safety is uncertain, they may vary, and interactions with other medicines have been reported. [[ref:nice-2026-ng23]]
items.body:
A 2012 Cochrane review cited by NAMS (16 trials, 2,027 women) found no difference between black cohosh and placebo in VMS frequency. Cases of possible hepatotoxicity have been reported, and an expert committee of the US Pharmacopeial Convention directed that these products carry a warning to stop them and seek advice if there is a liver disorder or liver symptoms appear. Soy studies are small, heterogeneous and short, and only 35% of North American women metabolise daidzein to equol. Also not recommended, among others, are pollen extract, ammonium succinate, wild yam, dong quai, evening primrose oil, maca, ginseng, chasteberry, milk thistle, omega-3 fatty acids, vitamin E and cannabinoids. [[ref:nams-2023-nonhormone-therapy]]

NICE notes that the safety, quality and purity of unregulated preparations may be unknown, and advises people with a history of, or at high risk of, breast cancer that, although St John’s wort may relieve VMS, there is uncertainty about dosage, persistence of effect, variation between preparations and serious interactions, for example with tamoxifen, anticoagulants and anticonvulsants. [[ref:nice-2026-ng23]]
items.recall: How does NAMS classify black cohosh and soy for VMS, and what does NICE say about them?
items.pearl: If a patient already takes black cohosh or St John’s wort, ask about liver symptoms and review her medicines: that is where the sources raise the alarm.

evidence.label: insufficient
evidence.note: NAMS 2023: black cohosh, Level I, not recommended; soy, soy extracts and equol, Level II, not recommended; supplements and herbal remedies as a group, Levels I-III, not recommended (table 2, p. 12; the abstract and conclusions say Levels I-II); cannabinoids, Level II, not recommended. NICE NG23 1.4.6, 1.4.7 and 1.4.8 [2015], which predate the 2023 statement: the sources disagree here. NAMS (now The Menopause Society) levels: I = good and consistent scientific evidence; II = limited or inconsistent scientific evidence; III = primarily consensus and expert opinion. NICE assigns no evidence levels to its recommendations; in brackets, the year each was made or updated.

items.title: Myth: exercise, yoga or cooling down treat hot flashes
items.core: NAMS does not recommend cooling techniques, avoiding triggers, exercise or yoga (Level II), or dietary modification (Level III), as treatment for VMS; it does consider weight loss for some women (Levels II-III). [[ref:nams-2023-nonhormone-therapy]]
items.body:
The Cochrane reviews cited found insufficient or poor evidence for exercise, which may even trigger VMS; in one study, hormone therapy was far more effective than exercise. A healthy diet is important for health, but there is limited evidence that it improves VMS. Data on weight loss come from small, non-randomised studies or post hoc analyses, and its effect may be greater early in the transition. [[ref:nams-2023-nonhormone-therapy]]

Acupuncture is not recommended either (Level II). Stellate ganglion block might relieve moderate to very severe VMS in selected women, weighing its risks as a procedure (Levels II-III, recommended). [[ref:nams-2023-nonhormone-therapy]]
items.recall: Which lifestyle measures does NAMS not recommend for VMS, and which does it consider?
items.application: Keep lifestyle advice for general health, but do not present it as treatment for hot flashes; if there is excess weight, weight loss is the exception NAMS does consider.

evidence.label: not-recommended
evidence.note: NAMS 2023: cooling, avoiding triggers, exercise and yoga, Level II, not recommended; diet, Level III, not recommended; weight loss, Levels II-III, recommended; acupuncture, Level II, not recommended; stellate ganglion block, Levels II-III, recommended. NICE NG23 gives no lifestyle recommendations for VMS in sections 1.4 and 1.5. NAMS (now The Menopause Society) levels: I = good and consistent scientific evidence; II = limited or inconsistent scientific evidence; III = primarily consensus and expert opinion.

items.stem: A 49-year-old woman (fictional case) on tamoxifen after breast cancer has bothersome VMS and wants a non-hormonal drug. According to NAMS, which of these is best avoided?

options.text: Paroxetine.
options.why: Correct: paroxetine, like fluoxetine, may inhibit the CYP2D6 that activates tamoxifen.

options.text: Venlafaxine.
options.why: It is one of the safer options with tamoxifen according to NAMS, owing to its smaller effect on CYP2D6.

options.text: Escitalopram.
options.why: NAMS includes it among the safer options with tamoxifen.

options.text: Desvenlafaxine.
options.why: It is also among the safer options with tamoxifen.

items.explanation: The interaction is not about efficacy on hot flashes but about oncological safety: inhibiting CYP2D6 reduces conversion of tamoxifen to endoxifen, its most active metabolite.

items.stem: A 50-year-old patient (fictional case) asks whether black cohosh will help her hot flashes. Which answer best reflects the sources?

options.text: NAMS does not recommend it (Level I, insufficient evidence); NICE, in 2015, mentions some evidence, but with uncertain safety and variable preparations.
options.why: Correct: it captures each source’s position and their disagreement.

options.text: Both sources recommend it as the first non-hormonal option.
options.why: NAMS does not recommend it and NICE does not propose it as a first option; it only informs, with caveats.

options.text: It is natural, so no precautions are needed.
options.why: Cases of possible hepatotoxicity and interactions with other medicines have been reported.

options.text: It is as effective as hormone therapy.
options.why: The Cochrane review cited by NAMS found no difference versus placebo in VMS frequency.

items.explanation: This is a point where the sources disagree: the NICE recommendation dates from 2015 and the 2023 NAMS statement reviewed later evidence. What they share is caution about safety and interactions.

items.stem: Which non-drug intervention does NAMS recommend for VMS at Level I?

options.text: Clinical hypnosis.
options.why: Correct: recommended at Level I, like CBT.

options.text: Paced respiration.
options.why: It has Level I, but for not recommending it: it was no better than controls.

options.text: Yoga.
options.why: Not recommended for VMS (Level II).

options.text: Acupuncture.
options.why: Not recommended for VMS (Level II).

items.explanation: In NAMS, the level indicates the quality of the evidence, not its direction: an option can have Level I and not be recommended, like paced respiration.

items.title: Case: Paloma, 51, hot flashes that keep her awake

steps.text: Paloma (fictional case), 51, healthy and not using hormonal contraception, has had no period for 14 months. She has several hot flashes a day and night sweats that wake her. Under NICE, menopause is identified clinically, without FSH or AMH. [[ref:nice-2026-ng23]]

She has a uterus, a BMI of 32 kg/m² and no history of thrombosis or cancer. She is offered HRT and benefits and risks are discussed. Because her BMI is over 30 kg/m², NICE proposes considering the transdermal route; NAMS adds that this advantage rests on observational studies. [[ref:nice-2026-ng23]] [[ref:nams-2022-hormone-therapy]]

As she has a uterus, transdermal estradiol with micronized progesterone is prescribed. For a cyclic regimen, NAMS gives 200 mg/day for 12–14 days a month as an example of an adequate dose; NICE notes that endometrial cancer risk decreases with continuous combined HRT and may increase slightly with sequential HRT, so the regimen is agreed with her. She is told that bleeding is common in the first 6 months and that treatment will be reviewed at 3 months and then annually. [[ref:nams-2022-hormone-therapy]] [[ref:nice-2026-ng23]]

A friend recommends “bioidentical” pellets dosed by saliva testing, plus black cohosh “just in case”. It is explained that the estradiol and micronized progesterone she already uses are bioidentical and regulated, that saliva testing cannot guide dosing, and that NAMS does not recommend black cohosh for VMS. [[ref:nams-2022-hormone-therapy]] [[ref:nams-2023-nonhormone-therapy]]

At 3 months she is sleeping better and asks how long she can continue and what about her breasts. It is explained that combined HRT slightly increases breast cancer risk, more with more years of use, and that NAMS considers it rare; that NICE asks for benefits and risks to be rediscussed at every review, and that NAMS sees no reason to stop it routinely at 60–65. If one day she could not use HRT, CBT, clinical hypnosis, SSRIs/SNRIs, gabapentin or fezolinetant would remain. [[ref:nice-2026-ng23]] [[ref:nams-2022-hormone-therapy]] [[ref:nams-2023-nonhormone-therapy]]

aemps-2026-mirena-ft.title: Fichas técnicas de Mirena 0,02 mg cada 24 horas y Levosert 0,02 mg cada 24 horas, sistemas de liberación intrauterinos (levonorgestrel 52 mg)
aemps-2026-mirena-ft.authors: AEMPS, CIMA; titulares Bayer Hispania y Gedeon Richter
aemps-2026-mirena-ft.population: Women using a 52 mg levonorgestrel IUD (Spain).
aemps-2026-mirena-ft.finding: Mirena: contraception (8 years) and idiopathic menorrhagia (5 years). Levosert: contraception and heavy menstrual bleeding. Neither includes endometrial protection during estrogen therapy.
aemps-2026-mirena-ft.limitations: Only Mirena sections 4.1 and 4.2 and Levosert section 4.1 were read (SmPCs dated 12 and 31 August 2026; nregistro 63158 and 80021); Levosert One was not read. Levosert SmPC: https://cima.aemps.es/cima/dochtml/ft/80021/FT_80021.html.

aemps-2026-progeffik-bijuva.title: Fichas técnicas de Progeffik 100 y 200 mg cápsulas blandas (progesterona) y Bijuva 1 mg/100 mg cápsulas blandas (estradiol/progesterona)
aemps-2026-progeffik-bijuva.population: Women with a uterus receiving estrogen; luteal insufficiency; luteal phase in assisted reproduction (Spain).
aemps-2026-progeffik-bijuva.finding: Oral Progeffik: adjunct to estrogen therapy in women with a uterus, among other indications; 200 mg/day for the last 2 weeks of each sequence. Vaginal route: luteal support in IVF and oocyte donation. Bijuva: continuous combined HRT in postmenopausal women with a uterus (≥ 12 months amenorrhoea).
aemps-2026-progeffik-bijuva.limitations: Progeffik sections 4.1 and 4.2 (SmPC dated 9 May 2019, old) and Bijuva 4.1 (SmPC dated 27 August 2026): https://cima.aemps.es/cima/dochtml/ft/85988/FT_85988.html.

aemps-2026-veoza-ft.title: Ficha técnica de Veoza 45 mg comprimidos recubiertos con película (fezolinetant)
aemps-2026-veoza-ft.authors: Agencia Española de Medicamentos y Productos Sanitarios (AEMPS), CIMA; titular Astellas Pharma Europe B.V.
aemps-2026-veoza-ft.population: Women with moderate to severe menopausal vasomotor symptoms (Spain/EU; centralised authorisation EMEA/H/C/005851).
aemps-2026-veoza-ft.finding: Indication: moderate to severe menopausal VMS; 45 mg once daily. Liver function tests before starting; do not start if ALT or AST ≥ 2 × ULN or total bilirubin is elevated; repeat monthly for the first 3 months and then as clinically indicated; stop if transaminases are ≥ 3 × ULN with bilirubin > 2 × ULN or symptoms, or > 5 × ULN.
aemps-2026-veoza-ft.limitations: Summary of product characteristics (not a guideline). Sections 4.1, 4.2 and 4.4 of the CIMA version were read (nregistro 1231771001; no revision date in the API). Medicine under additional monitoring.

anmat-2026-vnm.title: Vademécum Nacional de Medicamentos (consulta pública)
anmat-2026-vnm.authors: Administración Nacional de Medicamentos, Alimentos y Tecnología Médica (ANMAT), Argentina
anmat-2026-vnm.population: Medicine presentations listed in ANMAT’s National Medicines Formulary (Argentina).
anmat-2026-vnm.finding: Listed products include: Ethopil (dequalinium chloride 10 mg pessaries; cert. 60233); Utrogestan (micronized progesterone 100 and 200 mg; cert. 40881); Visanne (dienogest 2 mg); Mirena (levonorgestrel 20 µg/24 h); cabergoline 0.5 and 1 mg; prasterone 6.5 mg pessaries; folic acid 1, 5 and 10 mg.
anmat-2026-vnm.limitations: The search shows neither indications nor package leaflets. Generic-name search is exact-match, so no results does not prove absence of registration. Only the first page of results was read.

ema-2025-lynkuet-epar.title: Lynkuet (elinzanetant): EPAR – medicine overview
ema-2025-lynkuet-epar.authors: European Medicines Agency (EMA); titular Bayer AG
ema-2025-lynkuet-epar.population: Women with moderate to severe VMS (EU).
ema-2025-lynkuet-epar.finding: CHMP opinion 18 September 2025; EU marketing authorisation 17 November 2025 (EMEA/H/C/006298) for moderate to severe VMS; additional monitoring. In CIMA: Lynkuet 60 mg soft capsules, authorisation date 19 June 2026, not marketed as of 14 October 2026.
ema-2025-lynkuet-epar.limitations: EMA overview page and CIMA status; the full SmPC was not read (the CIMA PDF redirects to EMA).

fda-2026-veozah-label.title: VEOZAH (fezolinetant) tablets: prescribing information
fda-2026-veozah-label.authors: U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), DailyMed/openFDA; Astellas Pharma US
fda-2026-veozah-label.population: Women with moderate to severe VMS due to menopause (US).
fda-2026-veozah-label.finding: Boxed warning for postmarketing hepatotoxicity: baseline liver tests, do not start if aminotransferases or total bilirubin ≥ 2 × ULN, and monthly checks for the first 3 months and at 6 and 9 months.
fda-2026-veozah-label.limitations: US label (effective_time 26 February 2026) read via the openFDA API (boxed warning and section 2); not directly applicable to Spain or Argentina.

nams-2022-hormone-therapy.title: The 2022 hormone therapy position statement of The North American Menopause Society
nams-2022-hormone-therapy.authors: The 2022 Hormone Therapy Position Statement Advisory Panel of The North American Menopause Society (now The Menopause Society); Faubion SS (lead), Crandall CJ, Davis L, El Khoudary SR, Hodis HN, Lobo RA, Maki PM, Manson JE, Pinkerton JV, Santoro NF, Shifren JL, Shufelt CL, Thurston RC, Wolfman W
nams-2022-hormone-therapy.population: Perimenopausal and postmenopausal women considering hormone therapy, in the United States context (FDA indications). Position statement by an expert panel of The North American Menopause Society, approved by its Board of Trustees; Menopause 2022;29(7):767-794. Updates the 2017 statement.
nams-2022-hormone-therapy.finding: Hormone therapy is the most effective treatment for vasomotor symptoms and the genitourinary syndrome of menopause, and prevents bone loss and fracture. In women under 60 or within 10 years of menopause onset without contraindications, the benefit-risk ratio is favourable; when started after 60 or more than 10 years from menopause it appears less favourable because of greater absolute risks of coronary heart disease, stroke, venous thromboembolism and dementia. Women with a uterus need adequate progestogen. It does not need to be routinely stopped at 60–65. Compounded “bioidentical” hormones raise safety concerns, and saliva or urine testing to set the dose is unreliable.
nams-2022-hormone-therapy.limitations: Full PDF (28 pp.) read on the society's website. It is a consensus position statement, not a guideline with a formal systematic review: the “Key points” carry levels I (good and consistent evidence), II (limited or inconsistent) and III (consensus and expert opinion), with no separate strength grade. Much of the risk data comes from the WHI trials (oral conjugated equine estrogens and medroxyprogesterone acetate). US regulatory context. It was the current version as of 14-10-2026 (the society has published no later one).

nams-2023-nonhormone-therapy.title: The 2023 nonhormone therapy position statement of The North American Menopause Society
nams-2023-nonhormone-therapy.authors: The 2023 Nonhormone Therapy Position Statement Advisory Panel of The North American Menopause Society (now The Menopause Society); Shufelt CL (lead), Brown V, Carpenter JS, Chism LA, Faubion SS, Joffe H, Kling JM, Soares CN, Thurston RC
nams-2023-nonhormone-therapy.population: Women with menopausal vasomotor symptoms who are not good candidates for hormone therapy (contraindications such as estrogen-dependent cancers or cardiovascular disease) or prefer not to use it, including breast cancer survivors. Menopause 2023;30(6):573-590; updates the 2015 statement.
nams-2023-nonhormone-therapy.finding: Recommended: cognitive-behavioral therapy, clinical hypnosis, SSRIs/SNRIs, gabapentin and fezolinetant (Level I); oxybutynin (Levels I-II); weight loss and stellate ganglion block (Levels II-III). Not recommended: paced respiration (Level I); supplements and herbal remedies, including black cohosh (Levels I-III in table 2; I-II in the abstract); cooling techniques, avoiding triggers, exercise, yoga, mindfulness, relaxation, suvorexant, soy foods and extracts, equol, cannabinoids, acupuncture (Level II); clonidine (Levels I-III); dietary modification and pregabalin (Level III). Hormone therapy remains the most effective treatment.
nams-2023-nonhormone-therapy.limitations: Full PDF (18 pp.) read on the society's website; dosing table 1 (p. 6) and table 2 of recommendations with levels (p. 12). Consensus position statement with Levels I-III (no separate strength grade; each option is classified as “recommended” or “not recommended”). Many studies of non-drug options and supplements are small and use waitlist controls. It predates elinzanetant, still in development in 2023, and does not reflect any later labelling changes. It was the current version as of 14-10-2026.

nice-2026-ng23.title: Menopause: identification and management (NG23)
nice-2026-ng23.authors: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
nice-2026-ng23.population: People in perimenopause and menopause in the UK health system; section 1.7 covers premature ovarian insufficiency in people under 40. Published November 2015, last updated 15 April 2026.
nice-2026-ng23.finding: From age 45, identify perimenopause (recently started vasomotor symptoms and cycle changes) and menopause (no period for 12 months without hormonal contraception) clinically, without laboratory tests; do not use AMH, inhibins, oestradiol, antral follicle count or ovarian volume [2015]. Offer HRT for vasomotor symptoms [2015]; consider menopause-specific CBT [2024]; fezolinetant when HRT is unsuitable (TA1143); do not routinely offer SSRIs, SNRIs or clonidine as first-line treatment for vasomotor symptoms alone [2015]. Combined HRT with a uterus and oestrogen-only HRT after total hysterectomy, at the lowest effective dosage [2024], reviewed at 3 months and then annually [2015]. VTE risk is not increased with transdermal HRT but is with oral HRT; consider transdermal HRT if VTE risk is increased, including a BMI over 30 kg/m² [2015]. Breast cancer risk rises with combined HRT according to duration, and very little or not at all with oestrogen-only HRT [2024]. POI (1.7, 2015 recommendations): diagnosis with symptoms, including infrequent or absent periods, and raised FSH on 2 samples 4–6 weeks apart; do not diagnose on a single blood test or use AMH routinely. Offer replacement with HRT or a combined hormonal contraceptive, until at least the age of natural menopause unless contraindicated; HRT may have a more beneficial effect on blood pressure than a combined oral contraceptive; both offer bone protection; HRT is not a contraceptive.
nice-2026-ng23.limitations: Full PDF (105 pp., 15-04-2026 version) read. The POI recommendations have not been updated since 2015 and predate the 2024 ESHRE guideline (which requires a single FSH). It gives no numerical FSH threshold. UK health-system context.
